Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Martin Weber is a 60-year-old warehouse worker who came to treatment after years of trying to keep one part of his life sealed off from the rest. He grew up in an American family of European background and served in the military as a young man. When he speaks about the event that still defines his inner life, his words falter almost immediately. He will say that they were out in the field, that there was an attack, that men he knew did not come back, but then he stops, jaw tight, eyes fixed on the floor, and says he knows exactly what happened and still cannot find words that feel possible to say out loud. What is clearest is the moment of survival: he lived, and others did not. That fact has remained with him not as a simple memory but as something morally unbearable. When the event comes back to him, he does not remember it from a distance. He feels the same terror he felt then, sudden and total, as if the danger is not over but happening again.

In the months after he returned, Martin found that certain things were impossible to tolerate. Clothing that resembled what he had worn during his service came to feel contaminated by the event. He quietly got rid of some items and refused others without explaining why. Even in ordinary settings he would scan for details that reminded him of that period, and if a jacket, pair of boots, or work uniform looked too close, he would avoid it. He also learned very quickly that trying to think directly about what had happened left him overwhelmed with guilt and fear. So he built his days around not thinking. If his mind began moving in that direction, he would interrupt it, turn on the television, keep his hands busy, focus on a task, anything to shut the door before the memory took hold. Over time this became less a conscious decision than a way of living.

He also stayed away from places connected to what happened. He would not go near the location where the military event occurred, and over the years he structured his life so that no one would ask him to. When reunions, commemorations, or conversations raised the possibility, he found reasons not to attend. To other people this could look like stubbornness or privacy, but to Martin it felt necessary. He was certain that going there would bring everything back in a way he would not be able to control.

This way of living followed him into his work at the warehouse. The job suits him in some respects because it is physical and concrete, and there is comfort in stacking, moving, and counting things that stay where they are put. At the same time, the workplace regularly confronts him with reminders he has spent years trying to avoid. Standard issue work clothes, heavy boots, rows of uniforms or rugged outerwear coming through shipments, and the stark industrial environment can suddenly pull him toward the past. On those days he becomes quiet and rigid, focusing harder on the next pallet, the next box, trying not to let his mind drift. He does not explain this to coworkers. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous, that safety is temporary at best, and he moves through even ordinary days with that conviction in the background.

His partner has seen the cost of this narrowing. Martin does not talk about the event, not because it is unimportant but because the moment he approaches it he feels both terrified and ashamed. He believes he should have died too, or that there is something suspect in the fact that he survived when others did not. He often says, in one form or another, that he does not know who he is anymore. The man he was before the military feels inaccessible to him, and the man he has been since then feels organized around silence, caution, and guilt. His partner experiences him as present in practical ways but gone when anything emotional comes close to this subject.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a new trauma but the growing realization that he could no longer keep his life divided so neatly. A recent reminder at work left him shaken for hours, and when his partner later asked what had happened, he found himself once again unable to say it. That failure frightened him as much as the memory itself. At 60, Martin is tired of organizing his life around what he cannot wear, where he cannot go, and what he cannot let himself think about. At the same time, what frightens him most is that if he lets himself remember fully, the terror will be exactly as it was then, and the guilt of having survived will swallow whatever sense of self he has left. He comes to treatment hoping, cautiously, that there may be some way to speak about what happened without being overtaken by it.
